title: Holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:3)
hook: the preface ends and heaven and earth sing the same song

segments.voice: Yesterday, the offertory: bread and wine carried up, and a drop of water in the wine. Your line was the ordinary is carried up. Which dull task did you carry? Day one hundred and thirteen.

In the year King Ozias died, the prophet Isaiah says, he saw the Lord. He is in the Temple in Jerusalem, and what he sees, nobody could paint properly. The Lord, seated on a throne, high and elevated, and the edge of his robe filling the whole Temple. Above him stand fiery creatures called seraphim, each with six wings: two covering the face, two covering the feet, and two to fly. And they are calling out to each other, back and forth, so loud that the doorposts shake and the house fills with smoke. What they're calling is sung at every Mass, all over the world, today. Today's word is its name.
screen: `ISAIAH IN THE TEMPLE.` → `SERAPHIM WITH SIX WINGS.` → `THE DOORPOSTS SHAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's what they call, in the Douay-Rheims: "Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory." In Latin, the first word is Sanctus, holy, and that's the name of this moment at Mass. In Hebrew, the word is kadosh, and it means more than good or pure. It means set apart. Other. Not like anything else. Some readers hear in the triple repeat Hebrew's way of saying the utmost: holy beyond all holy. Now watch how the Mass gets there. After the gifts, the priest says: lift up your hearts. In Latin, Sursum corda. The people answer that they lift them up to the Lord. Then comes a prayer called the preface, giving thanks, and it ends by joining the angels and saints in their song. And the whole church sings the seraphim's words. Then it adds a second line, from Palm Sunday. When Jesus rode into Jerusalem, the crowds shouted, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord." With Hosanna on either side. So in one short song, the Temple vision and the Palm Sunday crowd meet. And the idea is that this isn't a copy. The church isn't imitating heaven. For a moment, Catholics believe, heaven and earth are singing the same song at the same time. The same verse is at the heart of a prayer in the synagogue, the Kedushah, so Jewish neighbors sing it too. In the book of Revelation, the creatures around the throne never stop singing it, day and night.
screen: `KADOSH: SET APART.` · `HOLY, THREE TIMES OVER.` · `LIFT UP YOUR HEARTS.` · `THE TEMPLE AND PALM SUNDAY MEET.` · then, large: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY, THE LORD GOD OF HOSTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: holy, three times. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say the word quietly three times, with a slow breath between each. Holy. Holy. Holy. Let each one go a little deeper than the last. If you don't pray, think of something in your life that feels set apart: a place, a memory, a person. Something you'd take your shoes off for. Just hold it, and let it be other. The bell holds the time.
Sanctus. Latin for holy: the seraphim's song from Isaiah, sung at every Mass as heaven and earth join in. Today's word.
Your line: heaven joins in. Today, when you hear people singing together, anywhere, a stadium, a car, a kitchen, notice it, and imagine the song is bigger than the room. Day one hundred and thirteen.

howItsDone: At the end of the preface, the whole congregation sings or says the Sanctus, joining the seraphim's words from Isaiah with the Palm Sunday Hosanna; in many churches everyone then kneels for the Eucharistic Prayer.

fork.setup: you're Isaiah, in the Temple. you see the Lord on a throne and seraphim crying holy until the doorposts shake. what do you say?
options: that you must build a greater temple.
that you're a man of unclean lips, and undone.
fork.reveal: Isaiah cries that he's undone, a man of unclean lips. a seraph touches his lips with a burning coal, and then he says: here I am, send me.

original.note: Hebrew: holy, set apart. Isaiah hears it three times.

trapdoor: what you thought: a song before the important part.
what it means: the church singing the seraphim's song with them, heaven and earth at once.
what a scholar hears: kadosh repeated three times, read by some as a superlative, the Trisagion of Isaiah 6:3, joined to Psalm 118's Benedictus via Matthew 21:9.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook's 'about seven hundred years before Jesus' replaced with the text's own marker (the year King Ozias died); 'a young man' cut (Isaiah 6 gives no age); KJV wording 'high and lifted up' replaced with the Douay-Rheims 'high and elevated'; the Hebrew-superlative claim softened to 'some readers hear'; 'the preface always ends the same way' corrected.
Douay-Rheims Isaiah 6:3 and Matthew 21:9 given from memory; confirm.
Isaiah's call dated c. 740 BC ('the year that king Ozias died'); 'about seven hundred years before Jesus' used. Confirm.
Hebrew repetition as superlative: a common explanation; confirm.
Fork reveal paraphrases Isaiah 6:5–8 (unclean lips, the coal, 'here I am, send me'); confirm the paraphrase.
Kedushah in Jewish liturgy includes Isaiah 6:3; mentioned briefly as a neighbor sharing the verse. Confirm tone.
'Lift up your hearts' and the preface's ending are described, not quoted from ICEL.
